items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Single-letter names carry the main logic: `BigInt a, b, c`, the struct field `uint32_t *d`, and `BigInt tmp`. There is no comment explaining the `#if 0` / `""""` / `// """` language-switching trick, even though the conventions ask for it. Formatting is otherwise clean.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: A stray binary `a.out` was committed. A hand-rolled BigInt (init/add/print) replaces the simple 64-bit loop the conventions call for. `n == 0` / `n == 1` are special-cased again before the loop. Python calls a redundant `sys.exit(0)` after `main()`. Functions are short.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The return values of `malloc` and `realloc` are never checked. Errors exit with no message at all (`if (argc < 2) return 1;`, `sys.exit(1)`). `strtoll` accepts trailing garbage such as "5abc" because only `endptr == argv[1]` is checked. Magic `cap = 16`. Python does catch the specific `ValueError`.

items.name: Boundary and large inputs
items.evidence: Both languages compute f(0)=0 and f(1)=1 iteratively. The C side uses an arbitrary-precision BigInt, so it is correct well past n=93. Missing, negative and non-numeric arguments all give a non-zero exit in both languages.

items.name: Exact invocation contract
items.evidence: `#if 0` is a Python comment, and the `""""`...`// """` string sits inside a C `#if 0` block or a `//` comment. It works with the exact commands given, with no invalid escapes and no stray C tokens. Each mode prints only the number.
